oggetti/ottante/cosa: A southern constellation of faint stars that contains the south celestial pole, the point around which the whole sky of the southern hemisphere seems to turn.
oggetti/ottante/quando: It cannot be seen from Italy; from the southern hemisphere at 34° south it never sets and can be seen every evening of the year, highest in September at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/ottante/dove: From Italy it never rises. From the southern hemisphere it is always towards the south, about a third of the way up the sky; to find the pole, extend the long arm of the Southern Cross.
oggetti/ottante/come: A faint constellation: you need a dark sky; σ Octantis, the 'southern pole star', is very close to the pole but is barely visible to the naked eye.
oggetti/ottante/origine: Octans is Latin for 'octant', a navigation instrument. Lacaille introduced it in 1751-52 as Octans Hadleianus.
oggetti/ottante/storia: The octant had been invented by John Hadley around 1730 to measure the height of stars and planets above the horizon at sea. Unlike the north, the south has no bright pole star: σ Octantis is only magnitude 5.4.
oggetti/ottante/stelle/0/significato: The brightest, even though it carries the letter Nu: it is an orange giant.
oggetti/ottante/stelle/1/significato: Second in brightness; you need a dark sky.
oggetti/ofiuco/cosa: A large constellation representing a man holding a snake (the constellation Serpens). Its main stars form a large, elongated pentagon.
oggetti/ofiuco/quando: Evenings from June to August, highest in July at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/ofiuco/dove: From Italy it is halfway up the sky towards the south, above Scorpius and Antares, below Hercules. From the southern hemisphere it can be seen in the north, halfway up the sky.
oggetti/ofiuco/come: With the naked eye; with binoculars, look for the globular clusters M10 and M12, two small smudges close together in the middle of the constellation.
oggetti/ofiuco/origine: Ophiuchus is Greek for 'serpent bearer'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/ofiuco/storia: It represents Asclepius, the healer who could bring the dead back to life, whom Zeus struck down with a thunderbolt; the snake was his symbol. The Sun passes through Ophiuchus between late November and mid-December, but it is not one of the signs of the zodiac. In 1604 Kepler's supernova appeared here.
oggetti/ofiuco/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic 'ra's al-hawwa', 'the head of the snake charmer'. A white star, close to the head of Hercules.
oggetti/ofiuco/stelle/1/significato: Two white stars very close together that look like a single one.
oggetti/ofiuco/stelle/2/significato: From the Arabic 'yad', 'hand', and the Latin 'prior', 'the first': it is the first of the two stars of the hand holding the snake. A red giant.
oggetti/ofiuco/stelle/3/significato: From the Arabic for 'the shepherd's dog'. An orange giant.
oggetti/pavone/cosa: A constellation of the southern sky representing a peacock. It has only one bright star, Peacock; the others are faint and form an unremarkable figure.
oggetti/pavone/quando: From the southern hemisphere it never sets; it is highest in August at around 9-10 pm, high in the southern sky.
oggetti/pavone/dove: From Italy it never rises. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it is high in the south and always stays above the horizon; it lies between Triangulum Australe and Tucana.
oggetti/pavone/come: With the naked eye for Peacock; binoculars show NGC 6752, a large globular cluster (a ball of hundreds of thousands of stars).
oggetti/pavone/origine: Pavo is Latin for 'peacock'. It was introduced by the Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman, and published by Plancius at the end of the 16th century.
oggetti/pavone/storia: It is one of the constellations that came from the first Dutch voyages to the East Indies, when sailors mapped the southern stars that cannot be seen from Europe. In Greek myth the peacock was the bird sacred to Hera.
oggetti/pavone/stelle/0/significato: The English for 'pavone' (the bird's Italian name). The name is modern: it was given in the 1930s for British navigation almanacs.
oggetti/pavone/stelle/1/significato: The constellation's second star, a white star easily visible to the naked eye.
oggetti/pavone/stelle/2/significato: A star similar to the Sun and fairly close to us.
oggetti/pegaso/cosa: A great winged horse, of which only the front half can be seen. You can recognise it by the Square of Pegasus, a large quadrilateral of four stars (one of them belongs to Andromeda).
oggetti/pegaso/quando: Evenings from September to November, highest in October at around 9 pm.
oggetti/pegaso/dove: From Italy it is high in the south. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it is seen low in the north, upside down. The Square is the starting point for finding Andromeda and Pisces.
oggetti/pegaso/come: With the naked eye for the Square; with binoculars, near Enif, you can see M15, a globular cluster that looks like a fuzzy little star.
oggetti/pegaso/origine: Pegasus is the winged horse of Greek myth. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/pegaso/storia: Pegasus was born from Medusa's blood when Perseus cut off her head. The hero Bellerophon rode him to defeat the Chimera. In 1995 the first planet around a Sun-like star, 51 Pegasi, was discovered right in this constellation.
oggetti/pegaso/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic for 'the nose': it is the horse's muzzle. An orange supergiant.
oggetti/pegaso/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic for 'the leg'. A red giant: it is the top right corner of the Square and its brightness changes a little.
oggetti/pegaso/stelle/2/significato: From Arabic, usually translated as 'the saddle'. A corner of the Square.
oggetti/pegaso/stelle/3/significato: From the Arabic for 'the flank'. It is the bottom left corner of the Square.
oggetti/perseo/cosa: The hero Perseus, holding the head of Medusa. You can recognise it by a curve of stars starting from Mirfak, between Cassiopeia and the Pleiades.
oggetti/perseo/quando: Evenings from December to February, highest in January at around 9 pm.
oggetti/perseo/dove: From Italy it passes very high, almost overhead. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) only part of it can be seen, low on the northern horizon. You can find it by following the 'W' of Cassiopeia towards the Pleiades.
oggetti/perseo/come: Naked eye and binoculars: between Perseus and Cassiopeia lies the Double Cluster (NGC 869 and NGC 884), two neighbouring heaps of stars, splendid through binoculars.
oggetti/perseo/origine: Perseus is the Greek hero, son of Zeus and Danaë. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/perseo/storia: Perseus cut off the head of Medusa, whose gaze turned people to stone, and then rescued Andromeda from the sea monster. Every August the Perseid shooting stars (known in Italy as the 'lacrime di San Lorenzo', 'the tears of St Lawrence') seem to come from this constellation.
oggetti/perseo/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic for 'the elbow'. A yellow supergiant at the centre of a group of stars visible through binoculars.
oggetti/perseo/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic 'ra's al-ghul', 'the demon's head': it is Medusa's eye. Roughly every 2 days and 21 hours it fades for a few hours, because a companion star eclipses it.
oggetti/fenice/cosa: A southern constellation representing the phoenix, the bird that rises again from its own ashes. It has only one fairly bright star, Ankaa; the others form a figure that is hard to recognise.
oggetti/fenice/quando: Evenings from October to December, highest in November at around 9 pm.
oggetti/fenice/dove: From Italy only part of it can be seen, very low on the southern horizon, below Cetus. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it passes almost overhead, near Achernar.
oggetti/fenice/come: With the naked eye; there are no easy objects for beginners, and from Italy it is too low: you need a clear, dark southern horizon.
oggetti/fenice/origine: Phoenix is the phoenix, the legendary bird. It was introduced by the Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman, and published by Plancius at the end of the 16th century.
oggetti/fenice/storia: In myth the phoenix lives for hundreds of years, then bursts into flames and is reborn from its ashes. It is one of the twelve constellations that came from the Dutch voyages to the East Indies.
oggetti/fenice/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic 'al-anqa', the name of a legendary bird, the equivalent of the phoenix. An orange giant.
oggetti/fenice/stelle/1/significato: The constellation's second star; through a telescope it is a double star.
oggetti/fenice/stelle/2/significato: A red giant, orange in colour.
oggetti/pittore/cosa: A small, faint southern constellation representing a painter's easel. It lies near Canopus, the second-brightest star in the sky.
oggetti/pittore/quando: From the southern hemisphere, evenings from December to February, highest in January at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/pittore/dove: From Italy it never rises. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it is high in the south, next to Canopus.
oggetti/pittore/come: With the naked eye; a faint constellation with no easy objects: you need a dark sky, far from towns.
oggetti/pittore/origine: Pictor is Latin for 'painter'. Lacaille introduced it in 1751-52 under the name 'the painter's easel'.
oggetti/pittore/storia: The French astronomer Lacaille mapped the southern sky from the Cape of Good Hope and gave the new constellations the names of instruments of the arts and sciences. A curious fact: around Beta Pictoris a disc of dust with planets was discovered, one of the first seen around another star.
oggetti/pittore/stelle/0/significato: The brightest star in the constellation, white.
oggetti/pittore/stelle/1/significato: A young star surrounded by a disc of dust where planets are forming; at least two have been discovered.
oggetti/pesci/cosa: A large zodiac constellation, but with faint stars: two fish tied together by a ribbon. You can recognise the 'Circlet', a small ring of stars below the Square of Pegasus.
oggetti/pesci/quando: Evenings from October to December, highest in November at around 9 pm.
oggetti/pesci/dove: From Italy it is high in the south, below the Square of Pegasus. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it can be seen in the north, halfway up the sky.
oggetti/pesci/come: A faint constellation: you need a dark sky, far from towns; binoculars show the Circlet nicely.
oggetti/pesci/origine: Pisces is Latin for 'fish' (plural). It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/pesci/storia: In Roman myth Venus and her son Cupid turned into fish and tied themselves together with a cord so as not to lose each other while fleeing from the monster Typhon. Today Pisces contains the point where the Sun is at the start of spring (the March equinox).
oggetti/pesci/stelle/0/significato: The brightest star in Pisces, a yellow giant.
oggetti/pesci/stelle/1/significato: Part of the Circlet, the small ring of stars below Pegasus.
oggetti/pesci/stelle/2/significato: From the Arabic for 'the cord': it is the knot that ties the two fish together. Through a telescope it is a double star.
oggetti/pesce-australe/cosa: A small southern constellation representing a fish. Almost all its light comes from a single star, Fomalhaut, which shines alone in a part of the sky with few stars.
oggetti/pesce-australe/quando: Evenings from September to November, highest in October at around 9 pm.
oggetti/pesce-australe/dove: From Italy it is low on the southern horizon: Fomalhaut is the only bright star in that area. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it passes almost overhead.
oggetti/pesce-australe/come: With the naked eye for Fomalhaut; otherwise it is a faint constellation with no easy objects.
oggetti/pesce-australe/origine: Piscis Austrinus is Latin for 'southern fish'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/pesce-australe/storia: On old charts the fish drinks the water that Aquarius pours from his jar. In Greek myth it was considered the father of the two fish of the constellation Pisces.
oggetti/pesce-australe/stelle/0/signific: From the Arabic 'fam al-hut', 'the mouth of the fish'. It is about 25 light years away and is surrounded by a ring of dust.
oggetti/pesce-australe/stelle/1/signific: A blue-white star, the second in the constellation.
oggetti/poppa/cosa: The stern of the ship Argo, a large constellation in the Milky Way. Its stars are scattered, with no easy shape; the northern part lies to the left of Sirius.
oggetti/poppa/quando: Evenings from January to March, highest in February at around 9 pm.
oggetti/poppa/dove: From Italy only the northern part can be seen, low on the southern horizon; the brightest stars stay right down on the horizon. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it is high, almost overhead.
oggetti/poppa/come: Binoculars: near the border with Monoceros are M46 and M47, two neighbouring open clusters, easy to see from Italy too.
oggetti/poppa/origine: Puppis is Latin for 'stern'. It was part of the great ship Argo, one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations, which Lacaille divided into three parts in the 18th century.
oggetti/poppa/storia: The Argo was the ship of Jason and the Argonauts, who set off in search of the golden fleece. The ship was so big in the sky that Lacaille divided it into Puppis, Vela and Carina, keeping the original Greek letters: that is why Puppis has neither an alpha nor a beta.
oggetti/poppa/stelle/0/significato: From the Greek for 'ship'. One of the hottest and most massive stars visible to the naked eye, blue in colour.
oggetti/poppa/stelle/1/significato: An orange supergiant, the second in the constellation.
oggetti/poppa/stelle/2/significato: A yellowish-white star whose brightness varies slightly as it pulsates.
oggetti/bussola/cosa: A small, faint constellation representing a mariner's compass. Three stars almost in a line, next to Puppis.
oggetti/bussola/quando: Evenings from February to April, highest in March at around 9 pm.
oggetti/bussola/dove: From Italy it is low on the southern horizon, below Hydra. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it is high, almost overhead.
oggetti/bussola/come: With the naked eye; a faint constellation with no easy objects: you need a dark sky, far from towns.
oggetti/bussola/origine: Pyxis is Latin for 'box', here meaning 'compass' (pyxis nautica). Lacaille introduced it in 1751-52.
oggetti/bussola/storia: Lacaille placed it next to the ship Argo, as a piece of the ship's equipment, even though the ancient Argonauts had no compass. A curious fact: T Pyxidis is here, a 'recurrent nova', a star that every so often suddenly flares up.
oggetti/reticolo/cosa: A small southern constellation, a diamond shape of faint stars. It lies near the Large Magellanic Cloud.
oggetti/reticolo/quando: From the southern hemisphere, evenings from November to January, highest in December at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/reticolo/dove: From Italy it never rises. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it is high in the south, between Achernar and the Large Magellanic Cloud.
oggetti/reticolo/come: With the naked eye; with good eyesight or binoculars Zeta Reticuli splits into two little stars close together, similar to the Sun.
oggetti/reticolo/origine: Reticulum is Latin for 'little net' and refers to the reticle, the grid of fine wires in a telescope's eyepiece. Lacaille introduced it in 1751-52.
oggetti/reticolo/storia: Lacaille dedicated it to the reticle he used to measure star positions from the Cape of Good Hope. Before him, another astronomer had placed a figure called the 'Rhombus' in this area.
oggetti/reticolo/stelle/0/significato: A yellow giant, the brightest star of the diamond.
oggetti/freccia/cosa: One of the smallest constellations in the sky: four stars that really do draw an arrow. It lies between Altair and Albireo, inside the Summer Triangle.
oggetti/freccia/quando: Evenings from July to September, highest in August at around 9 pm.
oggetti/freccia/dove: From Italy it is high in the south, a little above Altair. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it is seen low in the north.
oggetti/freccia/come: Binoculars: among the stars of the arrow is M71, a globular cluster that looks like a small smudge.
oggetti/freccia/origine: Sagitta is Latin for 'arrow'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/freccia/storia: In Greek myth it is often the arrow with which Hercules killed the eagle that tormented Prometheus. It is the third-smallest constellation in the sky.
oggetti/freccia/stelle/0/significato: The tip of the arrow: a red giant, orange in colour.
oggetti/freccia/stelle/1/significato: A red giant, in the middle of the arrow.
oggetti/freccia/stelle/2/significato: From the Arabic for 'arrow'. It lies in the tail of the arrow.
oggetti/sagittario/cosa: A centaur archer of the zodiac. Its main stars form the 'Teapot', a little pot with a spout and a handle, set in the richest part of the Milky Way.
oggetti/sagittario/quando: Evenings from July to September, highest in August at around 9 pm.
oggetti/sagittario/dove: From Italy it is low on the southern horizon; from southern Italy you can see all of it. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it passes almost overhead. It lies to the left of the tail of Scorpius.
oggetti/sagittario/come: Binoculars: above the spout of the Teapot is the Lagoon Nebula (M8), a cloud of gas that is visible even to the naked eye under a dark sky.
oggetti/sagittario/origine: Sagittarius is Latin for 'archer'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/sagittario/storia: For the Greeks it was a centaur (half man, half horse) with his bow aimed at Scorpius. In this direction lies the centre of our galaxy, the Milky Way, with its black hole.
oggetti/sagittario/stelle/0/significato: From 'qaws', Arabic for 'bow', and 'australis', Latin for 'southern': the southern part of the bow. It is the base of the Teapot.
oggetti/sagittario/stelle/1/significato: A very ancient name of Babylonian origin. A blue-white star in the handle of the Teapot.
oggetti/sagittario/stelle/2/significato: From the Latin for the archer's 'armpit'. A double star in the handle of the Teapot.
oggetti/sagittario/stelle/3/significato: From Arabic and Latin: 'the middle of the bow'. An orange giant.
oggetti/sagittario/stelle/4/significato: From Arabic and Latin: 'the northern part of the bow'. It is the lid of the Teapot.
oggetti/scultore/cosa: A very faint southern constellation with no recognisable shape. It lies between Fomalhaut and the tail of Cetus.
oggetti/scultore/quando: Evenings from October to December, highest in November at around 9 pm.
oggetti/scultore/dove: From Italy it is low on the southern horizon, to the left of Fomalhaut. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it passes almost overhead.
oggetti/scultore/come: Binoculars: under a dark sky you can see NGC 253, the Sculptor Galaxy, an elongated smudge and one of the brightest galaxies in the sky.
oggetti/scultore/origine: Sculptor is Latin for 'sculptor'. Lacaille introduced it in 1751-52 as 'the sculptor's workshop'.
oggetti/scultore/storia: Lacaille filled the southern sky with instruments of the arts and sciences, and this is one of those figures. A curious fact: the south pole of our galaxy lies here, so we are looking away from the Milky Way, towards lots of distant galaxies.
oggetti/scultore/stelle/0/significato: A blue-white star, the brightest in a very faint constellation.
oggetti/scudo/cosa: A small shield-shaped constellation with faint stars. It lies in a bright part of the Milky Way, above the northern part of Sagittarius.
oggetti/scudo/quando: Evenings from July to September, highest in August at around 9 pm.
oggetti/scudo/dove: From Italy it is in the south, halfway up the sky, below Aquila. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it is high towards the north.
oggetti/scudo/come: Binoculars: here is M11, the Wild Duck Cluster, a dense heap of stars; the Milky Way around it is extremely bright.
oggetti/scudo/origine: Scutum is Latin for 'shield'. It was introduced by the Polish astronomer Hevelius at the end of the 17th century.
oggetti/scudo/storia: Hevelius called it 'Sobieski's Shield' in honour of the King of Poland John III Sobieski, who won the Battle of Vienna in 1683. It is the only modern constellation dedicated to a real historical figure.
oggetti/scudo/stelle/0/significato: An orange giant, the brightest star in Scutum.
oggetti/serpente/cosa: A snake held by Ophiuchus. It is the only constellation split into two parts: the Head (to the right of Ophiuchus) and the Tail (to the left, towards Aquila).
oggetti/serpente/quando: Evenings from July to September, highest in August at around 9 pm.
oggetti/serpente/dove: From Italy it is in the south, halfway up the sky, around the large figure of Ophiuchus. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it can be seen in the north, halfway up the sky.
oggetti/serpente/come: Binoculars: in the Head is M5, a large globular cluster; in the Tail is the Eagle Nebula (M16), famous for the 'Pillars of Creation' photographed by the Hubble Space Telescope.
oggetti/serpente/origine: Serpens is Latin for 'serpent'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/serpente/storia: Ophiuchus is Asclepius, the god of medicine, and the snake is his symbol: it still appears in the symbol of medicine today. The IAU kept the constellation whole but split into two pieces, one on each side of Ophiuchus.
oggetti/serpente/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic for 'the serpent's neck'. An orange giant, in the Head.
oggetti/serpente/stelle/1/significato: An orange giant, the brightest star in the Tail.
oggetti/serpente/stelle/2/significato: A white star in the serpent's Head.
oggetti/sestante/cosa: A very faint constellation representing a sextant, the instrument for measuring angles. It lies below Regulus, the main star of Leo.
oggetti/sestante/quando: Evenings from March to May, highest in April at around 9 pm.
oggetti/sestante/dove: From Italy it is in the south, halfway up the sky, below Leo. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it is seen high in the north.
oggetti/sestante/come: A faint constellation with no easy objects: you need a dark sky, far from towns, and even then you will see only a few small stars.
oggetti/sestante/origine: Sextans is Latin for 'sextant'. It was introduced by the Polish astronomer Hevelius in 1687.
oggetti/sestante/storia: Hevelius dedicated it to the sextant he used to measure star positions in Danzig. In 1679 a fire destroyed his observatory and his instruments.
oggetti/sestante/stelle/0/significato: A white star, almost exactly on the celestial equator.
oggetti/sestante/stelle/1/significato: A faint star, visible only under a dark sky.
oggetti/toro/cosa: A bull of the zodiac: you can see the V-shaped head, with Aldebaran as its red eye, and two long horns. The Pleiades sit on its shoulder.
oggetti/toro/quando: Evenings from November to January, highest in December at around 9 pm.
oggetti/toro/dove: From Italy it is high in the south. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it can be seen in the north, fairly low and upside down. You can find it by following Orion's Belt to the right (and upwards).
oggetti/toro/come: Naked eye and binoculars: the Pleiades (M45), a cluster of blue stars, and the Hyades, the V-shaped cluster around Aldebaran.
oggetti/toro/origine: Taurus is Latin for 'bull'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/toro/storia: In myth Zeus turned himself into a white bull to carry off the princess Europa. Near the southern horn is the Crab Nebula (M1), the remains of a supernova seen by Chinese astronomers in 1054.
oggetti/toro/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic for 'the follower', because it seems to follow the Pleiades. An orange giant about 65 light years away: it is not part of the Hyades, it is closer.
oggetti/toro/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic for 'the one that butts with its horns': it is the tip of the northern horn, on the border with Auriga.
oggetti/toro/stelle/2/significato: The brightest star in the Pleiades. In myth she is one of the seven sisters, daughters of Atlas and Pleione.
oggetti/toro/stelle/3/significato: From the Chinese for 'heavenly gate'. It is the tip of the southern horn, near the Crab Nebula.
oggetti/telescopio/cosa: A small, very faint southern constellation representing a telescope. It lies below Corona Australis and Sagittarius.
oggetti/telescopio/quando: From the southern hemisphere, evenings from July to September, highest in August at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/telescopio/dove: From Italy it never rises: from Sicily and southern Italy you can glimpse part of it, skimming the southern horizon. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it is high, almost overhead.
oggetti/telescopio/come: A faint constellation with no easy objects: you need a dark sky, far from towns.
oggetti/telescopio/origine: Telescopium is Latin for 'telescope'. It was introduced by Lacaille in 1751-52.
oggetti/telescopio/storia: Lacaille dedicated many new constellations to scientific instruments, and the telescope could hardly be left out. It was originally larger, but some of its stars were later assigned to other constellations.
oggetti/telescopio/stelle/0/significato: A blue-white star, the only reasonably bright one in the constellation.
oggetti/triangolo/cosa: A small constellation: three stars forming a narrow, elongated triangle. It lies between Andromeda and Aries.
oggetti/triangolo/quando: Evenings from October to December, highest in November at around 9 pm.
oggetti/triangolo/dove: From Italy it passes very high, almost overhead. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it is seen low in the north.
oggetti/triangolo/come: Binoculars: under a very dark sky you can see M33, the Triangulum Galaxy, a large, faint smudge; it is one of the galaxies closest to us.
oggetti/triangolo/origine: Triangulum is Latin for 'triangle'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/triangolo/storia: The Greeks called it 'Deltoton', because it is shaped like the Greek letter delta (Δ). Together with M31 in Andromeda, the galaxy M33 is part of our 'Local Group' of galaxies.
oggetti/triangolo/stelle/0/significato: The brightest star in Triangulum, a white giant.
oggetti/triangolo/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic for 'the triangle'. A yellowish-white star, the tip of the triangle.
oggetti/triangolo/stelle/2/significato: A white star, the third corner of the triangle.
oggetti/triangolo-australe/cosa: A small southern constellation: three fairly bright stars forming an almost perfect triangle. It lies near Alpha and Beta Centauri.
oggetti/triangolo-australe/quando: From the southern hemisphere it never sets; it is highest in July at around 9-10 pm, high in the southern sky.
oggetti/triangolo-australe/dove: From Italy it never rises. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it is high in the south and always stays above the horizon; you can find it next to the 'Pointers' of Centaurus, which point to the Southern Cross.
oggetti/triangolo-australe/come: Binoculars: here is NGC 6025, an open cluster near the northern side of the triangle.
oggetti/triangolo-australe/origine: Triangulum Australe is Latin for 'southern triangle'. It was introduced at the end of the 16th century by the Dutch navigators (Plancius, Keyser and de Houtman).
oggetti/triangolo-australe/storia: It came from the first Dutch voyages to the East Indies, when sailors mapped the southern stars. Unlike the northern Triangulum, it has no myth: it is just a geometric figure that is easy to see.
oggetti/triangolo-australe/stelle/0/sign: The name is a contraction of 'Alpha Trianguli Australis'. An orange giant.
oggetti/triangolo-australe/stelle/1/sign: A yellowish-white star, a corner of the triangle.
oggetti/triangolo-australe/stelle/2/sign: A white star, a corner of the triangle.
oggetti/tucano/cosa: A southern constellation representing the toucan, the bird with the big beak. Its stars are faint, but this is where you find the Small Magellanic Cloud, a nearby galaxy visible to the naked eye.
oggetti/tucano/quando: From the southern hemisphere it never sets; it is highest in October at around 9-10 pm, high in the southern sky.
oggetti/tucano/dove: From Italy it never rises. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it is high in the south and always stays above the horizon, near Achernar.
oggetti/tucano/come: Naked eye and binoculars: the Small Magellanic Cloud and, next to it, 47 Tucanae (NGC 104), one of the brightest globular clusters in the sky.
oggetti/tucano/origine: Tucana is Latin for 'toucan'. It was introduced by the Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman, and published by Plancius at the end of the 16th century.
oggetti/tucano/storia: It is one of the twelve constellations that came from the Dutch voyages to the East Indies. The toucan lives in South America: the navigators knew it from travellers' tales and drawings.
oggetti/tucano/stelle/0/significato: An orange giant, the only bright star in the constellation.
oggetti/orsa-minore/cosa: A small bear with a long tail. Its seven stars form the Little Dipper, which ends with the Pole Star, the fixed point of the sky towards the north.
oggetti/orsa-minore/quando: It can be seen all year round because from Italy it never sets; highest in June at around 9 pm.
oggetti/orsa-minore/dove: From Italy it is in the north, halfway up the sky: the Pole Star always stays in the same place and shows you where north is. It cannot be seen from the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America). You can find it by extending the distance between Merak and Dubhe in the Plough about five times.
oggetti/orsa-minore/come: With the naked eye; there are no easy objects, but its faint stars are a good test: if you can see the whole Little Dipper, the sky is truly dark.
oggetti/orsa-minore/origine: Ursa Minor is Latin for 'lesser she-bear'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/orsa-minore/storia: According to Greek writers, Phoenician sailors steered by Ursa Minor, the Greeks by Ursa Major. Polaris will not be the pole star for ever: the Earth slowly wobbles like a spinning top, and thousands of years from now the pole will point to other stars, such as Vega.
oggetti/orsa-minore/stelle/0/significato: It is less than one degree from the north celestial pole, so it seems to stand still while the sky turns. It is a yellow supergiant that pulsates slightly.
oggetti/orsa-minore/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic for 'the star'. An orange giant: together with Pherkad it forms the 'Guardians of the Pole'.
oggetti/orsa-minore/stelle/2/significato: From the Arabic for 'the calf'. A white giant, one of the 'Guardians of the Pole'.
oggetti/vela/cosa: The sails of the ship Argo, a southern constellation set in the Milky Way. Two of its stars, together with two from Carina, form the 'False Cross', often mistaken for the Southern Cross.
oggetti/vela/quando: Evenings from February to April, highest in March at around 9 pm.
oggetti/vela/dove: From Italy only part of it can be seen, skimming the southern horizon: from southern Italy you can make out a few more stars. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it is high, almost overhead.
oggetti/vela/come: Naked eye and binoculars: from the southern hemisphere there is IC 2391, an open cluster of bright stars around Omicron Velorum.
oggetti/vela/origine: Vela is Latin for 'sails'. It was part of the great ship Argo, one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations, which Lacaille divided into three parts in the 18th century.
oggetti/vela/storia: The Argo was the ship of Jason and the Argonauts. Lacaille divided it into Puppis, Vela and Carina, keeping the original Greek letters: that is why Vela has neither an alpha nor a beta.
oggetti/vela/stelle/0/significato: A name that began as a joke: it is 'Roger' spelt backwards, in honour of the astronaut Roger Chaffee. It is the brightest Wolf-Rayet star (a type of extremely hot star) in the sky.
oggetti/vela/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic for 'the ship'. It is part of the False Cross.
oggetti/vela/stelle/2/significato: An ancient Arabic name used for several bright southern stars. An orange supergiant.
oggetti/vela/stelle/3/significato: From the Arabic for 'vehicle' or 'ship'. It is part of the False Cross.
oggetti/vergine/cosa: A large zodiac constellation, the second largest in the sky. The easiest star is Spica, blue-white; the others form a faint 'Y'.
oggetti/vergine/quando: Evenings from April to June, highest in May at around 9 pm.
oggetti/vergine/dove: From Italy it is in the south, halfway up the sky. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it can be seen in the north, halfway up the sky. To find Spica, follow the curve of the Plough's handle to Arcturus and then keep going.
oggetti/vergine/come: With the naked eye for Spica; the Virgo Cluster, thousands of galaxies, is here, but you need a telescope and a dark sky.
oggetti/vergine/origine: Virgo is Latin for 'virgin' or 'maiden'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/vergine/storia: For the Greeks she was often Astraea, goddess of justice (nearby Libra was her pair of scales), or Demeter, goddess of the harvest, holding an ear of wheat. Virgo contains the point where the Sun is at the start of autumn (the September equinox).
oggetti/vergine/stelle/0/significato: Latin for an 'ear' of wheat, the one Virgo holds in her hand. It is a pair of hot blue stars very close together.
oggetti/vergine/stelle/1/significato: Porrima was a Roman goddess of prophecy. Through a telescope it is a double star: two twin stars orbiting each other.
oggetti/vergine/stelle/2/significato: Latin for 'the grape-harvester': in ancient times it rose before dawn during the grape harvest. A yellow giant.
oggetti/pesce-volante/cosa: A small southern constellation representing a flying fish. Its faint stars lie near Carina, north of the Large Magellanic Cloud.
oggetti/pesce-volante/quando: From the southern hemisphere it never sets; it is highest in February at around 9-10 pm, high in the southern sky.
oggetti/pesce-volante/dove: From Italy it never rises. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it is high in the south and always stays above the horizon, between Canopus and the Large Magellanic Cloud.
oggetti/pesce-volante/come: With the naked eye; a faint constellation with no easy objects: you need a dark sky, far from towns.
oggetti/pesce-volante/origine: Volans is Latin for 'flying', short for 'Piscis Volans', 'flying fish'. It was introduced by the Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman, and published by Plancius at the end of the 16th century.
oggetti/pesce-volante/storia: The Dutch navigators saw flying fish leaping out of the water in tropical seas and put them in the sky. On old charts the flying fish is often being chased by the Dorado, the fish of the neighbouring constellation.
oggetti/pesce-volante/stelle/0/significa: An orange giant, the brightest star in the constellation.
oggetti/pesce-volante/stelle/1/significa: An orange giant; a small telescope shows that it has a close companion.
oggetti/volpetta/cosa: A small, faint constellation representing a fox. It lies inside the Summer Triangle, above Sagitta, and has no recognisable shape.
oggetti/volpetta/quando: Evenings from July to September, highest in August at around 9 pm.
oggetti/volpetta/dove: From Italy it is high in the south, almost overhead. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it is seen low in the north.
oggetti/volpetta/come: Binoculars: here is the Coathanger (Collinder 399), a line of stars with a hook, very easy to recognise; nearby is also the Dumbbell Nebula (M27).
oggetti/volpetta/origine: Vulpecula is Latin for 'little fox'. It was introduced by the Polish astronomer Hevelius in 1687 as 'Vulpecula cum Ansere', the little fox with the goose.
oggetti/volpetta/storia: Originally the fox held a goose in its mouth; today the goose survives only in the name of the brightest star. A curious fact: in 1967 Jocelyn Bell discovered the first pulsar here, a dead star that spins extremely fast and sends out regular radio pulses.
oggetti/volpetta/stelle/0/significato: Latin for 'goose', the goose the fox held in its mouth. A red giant.
